title: Pay Students To Go To School? (Bad Pandemic Recovery Idea #42,231)
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene critiques a Hechinger Report proposal to use ESSER funds to pay students sixteen and older to attend after-school enrichment, summer learning and in-school jobs as a response to pandemic learning loss. He first challenges the premise, noting that measuring lost learning in weeks is just restating that test scores are down. His main objections are practical and motivational: extrinsic payment tends to erode intrinsic interest, it implicitly admits there is no good reason to attend, and the school-job idea amounts to child labor with surveillance side benefits. He closes with a porch analogy asking why schools would not simply rebuild what worked before the pandemic. The post is a representative piece of his school-policy commentary on how badly the case for school attendance is being argued.
points: Offering a stipend signals that the school has no intrinsic reason for students to attend, which is exactly the wrong message.
Extrinsic payment risks reducing motivation and raises fairness problems when regular school remains unpaid.
You can pay a student to show up but not to care; the bribe itself shows there is no reason offered to care.
Claims that learning loss can be counted in weeks are a dressed-up way of saying test scores fell.
quotes: Anyone who claims they can measure learning in weeks or months or years or hectares or liters is just shoveling baloney. What they actually mean is "test scores are down," but you can't get people worked up about that.

This is great language, but we're mostly talking about paying students to go to school, and the problems I see are many. "Why am I getting paid to go to summer school but I have to go to regular school for free," ask a few million students. Add to that the problems that arise from using extrinsic motivation with students (eg actually decreasing motivation and interest).

But most of all, this strikes me as simple admission that there's no good reason, no intrinsic reward available for going to extra school in order to raise some test scores. "We have no good argument for why you should give up part of your life so that test scores will go up," we're admitting. "How about a twenty?

Yes, I'd say turning a privilege and right and a public good into a job would be seismic. Nor is it clear to me that this would help, because I'm pretty sure the proposition would be heard, correctly, by many students as, "So you'll pay me to come sit in this summer school class.

So I'm highly doubtful that the damage done by this scheme would even yield the higher test scores he's hoping for. You can pay a student to show up, but you can't pay her to care--and the mere fact that you're offering to bribe her to show up is a clear indication that there is no reason for her to care.

If I build a porch on my house, and then some jerk comes along with a bulldozer and knocks the porch down, why would I declare, "Well, the house now looks like it did in the pre-porch days. I guess now I'll have to build a garage or a rowboat on the front." Why would I not just build back the perfectly good porch I had built there before?
